title: Programming Foundations & Logic
description: Understand how computers store data, evaluate truth, and make decisions using core logic.

cards.front: What happens in computer memory when you declare a variable?
cards.back: The program reserves a labeled spot in RAM to store a value so you can read, update, or reuse it later by name.

cards.front: Why does '10' + '5' equal '105' instead of 15 in most programming languages?
cards.back: Because values wrapped in quotes are Strings (text), so the + operator concatenates (joins) them together rather than doing math.

cards.front: What is type coercion, and why can it cause unexpected bugs?
cards.back: It is when a language automatically converts one data type to another (like turning a number into a string), which can cause weird comparisons like '5' == 5 evaluating to true.

cards.front: How do logical operators AND (&&) and OR (||) differ in an if-statement?
cards.back: AND (&&) requires every condition to be true to run, while OR (||) runs as long as at least one condition is true.

cards.front: What is the modulo (%) operator used for in coding?
cards.back: It returns the remainder of a division problem—commonly used to check if a number is even or odd (num % 2 === 0).

title: Loops & Control Flow
description: Master how programs repeat actions efficiently without writing duplicate code.

cards.front: What causes an infinite loop, and how does it affect your browser or program?
cards.back: It happens when a loop's exit condition never becomes false, causing the program to run forever and freeze the browser tab.

cards.front: What is the difference between the 'break' and 'continue' keywords inside a loop?
cards.back: 'break' exits the entire loop immediately, while 'continue' skips just the current iteration and jumps to the next cycle.

cards.front: Why do arrays use zero-based indexing (starting at 0 instead of 1)?
cards.back: The index represents the offset distance from the very first item in memory—the first item is 0 steps away from the start.

cards.front: What is a 'nested loop', and when would you use one?
cards.back: A loop placed inside another loop, commonly used to work with 2D grids, tables, or arrays inside arrays.

cards.front: How does a 'for...of' loop (or Python 'for item in list') make code cleaner?
cards.back: It lets you directly access each item in a list without manually tracking index numbers like i = 0 or i++.

title: Functions & Scope
description: Learn how to package reusable code blocks and control where variables can be accessed.

cards.front: What is the difference between a function's parameters and arguments?
cards.back: Parameters are the placeholder variable names in the function definition; arguments are the actual values you pass in when calling it.

cards.front: Why is returning a value from a function usually better than just printing it with console.log()?
cards.back: Returning sends the result back to your code so other functions can save or use it; console.log() only displays text for humans to read.

cards.front: What is variable 'scope' in programming?
cards.back: The region of your code where a variable exists and can be accessed—variables created inside a function stay trapped inside that function.

cards.front: Why should you avoid creating too many global variables?
cards.back: Any part of your program can accidentally overwrite a global variable, leading to hard-to-trace bugs as your project grows.

cards.front: What is a 'pure function'?
cards.back: A function that always produces the exact same output for the same inputs and does not modify anything outside of itself.

title: Data Structures Essentials
description: Organize complex collections of information using arrays, objects, stacks, and queues.

cards.front: When should you store data in an Object (Key-Value) instead of an Array (List)?
cards.back: Use an Array when the order of items matters; use an Object when you want to look up properties by a descriptive name (like user.email).

cards.front: What is an 'Array of Objects', and why is it the backbone of most apps?
cards.back: A list where every item is a structured object—ideal for storing collections like a list of flashcard sets or user profiles.

cards.front: How does a Stack data structure work (LIFO)?
cards.back: Last-In, First-Out—the most recently added item is the first one removed, just like a stack of plates or your browser's Back button.

cards.front: How does a Queue data structure work (FIFO)?
cards.back: First-In, First-Out—items are processed in the exact order they arrived, just like a line at a ticket counter.

cards.front: What does 'mutating' data mean, and why do developers watch out for it?
cards.back: Mutating means changing an existing array or object directly in memory rather than making a fresh copy, which can cause unintended side effects.

title: Modern HTML & Accessibility
description: Build meaningful webpage skeletons that work seamlessly for all users and search engines.

cards.front: What is the purpose of the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration at the top of an HTML file?
cards.back: It tells the browser to render the page using modern HTML5 standards instead of falling back into outdated compatibility modes.

cards.front: Why should every tag include a descriptive 'alt' attribute?
cards.back: Screen readers read the alt text aloud to visually impaired users, and it displays on screen if the image fails to load.

cards.front: What is the <meta name='viewport'> tag responsible for?
cards.back: It instructs mobile browsers to match the webpage's width to the device's screen width so text isn't zoomed out tiny.

title: CSS Layouts & Styling
description: Control spacing, alignment, responsiveness, and visual polish on the web.

cards.front: What does 'box-sizing: border-box;' fix in CSS?
cards.back: It forces an element's width and height to include its padding and border, preventing boxes from unexpectedly growing larger than set.

cards.front: When should you use CSS Grid instead of Flexbox?
cards.back: Use Flexbox for 1-dimensional layouts (a single row or column); use CSS Grid for 2-dimensional layouts (rows and columns simultaneously).

cards.front: What is CSS Specificity, and why do some styles fail to apply?
cards.back: It is the scoring system browsers use to decide which CSS rule wins—IDs (#header) override classes (.card), which override element tags (div).

cards.front: What is the difference between 'rem' and 'px' units in CSS?
cards.back: 'px' is a fixed pixel size, while 'rem' scales relative to the root font size—making your site respect users' browser accessibility settings.

cards.front: How do CSS Media Queries enable responsive design?
cards.back: They apply specific CSS rules only when conditions are met, such as @media (max-width: 768px) for tablets and phones.

title: JavaScript & The DOM
description: Connect your JavaScript logic to HTML elements to create interactive web apps.

cards.front: What is the difference between innerText and innerHTML?
cards.back: innerText inserts plain text safely, while innerHTML parses HTML tags—using innerHTML with untrusted user input can expose your site to security attacks.

cards.front: How does element.classList.toggle('flipped') work?
cards.back: It adds the 'flipped' CSS class if it is missing from the element, and removes it if it is already there—perfect for card flip animations.

cards.front: What is 'Event Delegation' in JavaScript?
cards.back: Attaching a single event listener to a parent container instead of dozens of individual child buttons, saving memory and handling dynamically created items.

cards.front: What does event.preventDefault() do on a form submission?
cards.back: It stops the browser's default behavior of refreshing the entire webpage when a form is submitted, letting JavaScript handle the data smoothly.

title: Asynchronous JS & APIs
description: Understand how websites fetch external data without freezing the user interface.

cards.front: Why does JavaScript need asynchronous code for tasks like fetching data?
cards.back: JavaScript runs on a single thread—if it waited synchronously for a slow network request, the entire webpage would freeze until it finished.

cards.front: What is a JavaScript 'Promise'?
cards.back: An object representing the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation, existing in one of three states: pending, fulfilled, or rejected.

cards.front: Why do you have to call response.json() after using fetch('data.json')?
cards.back: fetch() returns a raw HTTP response stream first; .json() reads that stream and parses the text into usable JavaScript objects.

cards.front: How do 'async' and 'await' improve working with Promises?
cards.back: They let you write asynchronous code that reads cleanly from top to bottom like normal code, avoiding messy chains of .then() callbacks.

cards.front: What do HTTP status codes 200, 404, and 500 tell you?
cards.back: 200 means the request succeeded; 404 means the requested file or route was not found; 500 means the server crashed or hit an internal error.

title: Browser Storage & Web Security
description: Save user progress locally and protect your web applications from common vulnerabilities.

cards.front: Why must you use JSON.stringify() before saving an array or object into localStorage?
cards.back: Because localStorage can only store plain strings—saving a raw object turns it into the useless text '[object Object]'.

cards.front: What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
cards.back: localStorage keeps data saved even after the browser is closed, whereas sessionStorage wipes the data as soon as that browser tab is closed.

cards.front: What is CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), and why does it block local file fetches?
cards.back: It is a browser security rule preventing websites from silently reading files from your computer's hard drive or unauthorized external domains.

cards.front: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)?
cards.back: A security vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a webpage (often via unescaped form inputs) that runs in other users' browsers.

cards.front: Why should you never store secret API keys or passwords inside frontend JavaScript files?
cards.back: Anyone visiting your website can open Browser DevTools, view your source files, and steal any keys written in frontend code.

title: Developer Workflow & Clean Code
description: Adopt professional debugging habits, version control practices, and readable code principles.

cards.front: What is the standard three-step Git workflow to save your progress?
cards.back: 1. 'git add .' (stage changes), 2. 'git commit -m "message"' (save a snapshot), and 3. 'git push' (upload to GitHub).

cards.front: What is a '.gitignore' file used for?
cards.back: It tells Git which local files or folders (like API secret files, OS junk, or heavy dependency folders) should never be uploaded to GitHub.

cards.front: Why are descriptive variable names better than short ones like 'x' or 'data2'?
cards.back: Code is read far more often than it is written—clear names like 'currentCardIndex' act as built-in documentation for your future self.

cards.front: What does 'separation of concerns' mean in web development?
cards.back: Keeping structure (HTML), presentation (CSS), and behavior (JS) in separate, focused files so changing one doesn't break the others.

cards.front: When debugging a broken feature, why should you isolate the problem first?
cards.back: Testing one small piece at a time (e.g., logging fetched data before rendering HTML) pinpoints the exact failure instead of guessing.

title: Modern JavaScript (ES6+)
description: Write cleaner, shorter, and more readable JavaScript using modern syntax features.

cards.front: How do Template Literals (backticks ``) improve working with strings in JavaScript?
cards.back: They let you embed variables directly inside strings using ${variable} and write multi-line text without messy + concatenation.

cards.front: What is Array or Object Destructuring?
cards.back: A shorthand syntax that unpacks values from arrays or properties from objects directly into distinct variables (e.g., const { title, cards } = set).

cards.front: What does the Spread Operator (...) do when working with arrays or objects?
cards.back: It expands an array or object into individual elements, making it easy to clone data or merge two arrays together without mutating the original.

cards.front: How do Arrow Functions (() => {}) differ in syntax from traditional functions?
cards.back: They offer a shorter syntax and allow implicit returns—if the function is a single expression, you can omit the curly braces and the 'return' keyword.

cards.front: What do the array methods .map() and .filter() have in common?
cards.back: Both loop through an array and return a brand-new array without modifying the original—.map() transforms every item, while .filter() keeps only items that pass a test.

title: Problem Solving & Algorithms
description: Learn how programmers break down tricky challenges and write efficient logic.

cards.front: What is Pseudocode, and why do experienced developers write it first?
cards.back: Writing out your program's step-by-step logic in plain English before touching real code, helping you solve the problem without worrying about syntax rules.

cards.front: What are 'Edge Cases' in programming?
cards.back: Unusual or extreme inputs—like an empty flashcard array, a negative number, or special characters—that can crash code if you only tested normal inputs.

cards.front: Why is Binary Search so much faster than Linear Search on a sorted list?
cards.back: Linear Search checks items one by one from start to finish, while Binary Search repeatedly cuts the remaining search area in half.

cards.front: What does Big O Notation measure in computer science?
cards.back: How a piece of code's runtime or memory usage scales as the input size grows—for example, whether 10,000 items takes 10,000 steps or 100,000,000 steps.

cards.front: What is Recursion in programming?
cards.back: When a function calls itself to solve smaller versions of the same problem until it reaches a stopping condition called a 'base case'.

title: How the Internet & Web Work
description: Understand what actually happens behind the scenes when a browser loads a website.

cards.front: What is DNS (Domain Name System), and why is it called the phonebook of the internet?
cards.back: It translates human-friendly domain names (like google.com) into the numerical IP addresses computers use to locate servers.

cards.front: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
cards.back: HTTPS adds SSL/TLS encryption to HTTP, scrambling data sent between the browser and server so attackers on public Wi-Fi cannot read it.

cards.front: What happens in the Client-Server model when you click a link?
cards.back: Your browser (the client) sends an HTTP request over the internet, and a remote computer (the server) responds with the HTML, CSS, JS, and data files.

cards.front: What is the difference between a GET request and a POST request?
cards.back: GET asks a server to retrieve and send back data (like loading flashcards), while POST sends new data to a server to be created or saved (like submitting a signup form).

cards.front: What is Web Hosting, and how do free static hosts like GitHub Pages or Netlify work?
cards.back: Web hosting stores your website's files on an always-on server connected to the internet so anyone with the URL can visit your site.

title: Backend & Databases Basics
description: Explore how servers, databases, and authentication work behind the user interface.

cards.front: Why can't a frontend-only website share user-created flashcards across different devices?
cards.back: Because frontend storage like localStorage lives strictly inside one browser on one device—sharing data across users requires a central backend server and database.

cards.front: What is the difference between SQL (Relational) and NoSQL (Document) databases?
cards.back: SQL databases store structured data in strict tables with rows and columns (like spreadsheets), while NoSQL databases store flexible JSON-like documents.

cards.front: What does CRUD stand for in backend development?
cards.back: Create, Read, Update, and Delete—the four fundamental operations every database-driven application performs on data.

cards.front: What is an Environment Variable (.env file)?
cards.back: A hidden configuration file kept on the server to store sensitive secrets like database passwords and API keys safely outside of your public code.

cards.front: What is the difference between Authentication and Authorization?
cards.back: Authentication verifies who you are (logging in with a password), while Authorization checks what you are allowed to do (like editing only your own decks).

title: UI/UX & Interactive App Design
description: Design intuitive, responsive interfaces that feel smooth and enjoyable to use.

cards.front: What is 'State' in an interactive web application?
cards.back: Any data that changes over time while a user interacts with your app—such as which set is selected, the current card index, and whether a card is flipped.

cards.front: Why should you disable or loop the 'Previous' button when the user is on the first flashcard?
cards.back: Preventing invalid actions stops users from hitting out-of-bounds array errors (index -1) and gives clear visual feedback about where they are.

cards.front: How does CSS 'transition' make UI interactions feel smoother?
cards.back: Instead of snapping abruptly from one style to another on hover or click, 'transition' animates the property change gradually over a set duration (e.g., 0.3s).

cards.front: Why is adding keyboard shortcuts (like Spacebar to flip and Arrow keys for Next/Prev) great UX?
cards.back: Power users can study much faster without moving their mouse, and it makes your web app feel like a polished native application.

cards.front: What are 'Empty States' and 'Loading States' in UI design?
cards.back: Visual placeholders—like a 'Loading flashcards...' spinner or 'No cards found' message—that reassure users the app is working rather than broken.
